title: General Chemistry (CHM 101/102)
description: Atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, acids and bases, and an introduction to organic chemistry for 100 Level health science students.

topics.title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
topics.summary: Subatomic particles, isotopes, electronic configuration and periodic trends.

notes.b: An atom has a nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral) surrounded by electrons (negative). The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons; the mass number (A) is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons (e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14; iodine-131 is used in thyroid therapy). Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy (Aufbau principle): 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d …; each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin (Pauli exclusion principle) and electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly first (Hund's rule).

Across a period (left to right) atomic radius decreases while ionisation energy and electronegativity increase, because nuclear charge increases with electrons added to the same shell. Down a group, atomic radius increases and ionisation energy decreases because of extra shells and shielding. Group 1 are alkali metals, group 17 halogens, group 18 noble gases. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
k: Across a period: radius ↓, ionisation energy ↑, electronegativity ↑
Down a group: radius ↑, ionisation energy ↓

topics.title: Chemical Bonding and Intermolecular Forces
topics.summary: Ionic, covalent, coordinate and metallic bonds, molecular shapes and hydrogen bonding.

notes.b: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer between metals and non-metals (e.g. NaCl) and give high-melting solids that conduct when molten or dissolved. Covalent bonds form by sharing electron pairs between non-metals (e.g. H2O, CH4). A coordinate (dative) bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons come from one atom (e.g. NH4+, H3O+). Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.
k: Dative bond: both electrons from one atom (NH4+)

notes.b: VSEPR theory predicts shape from electron pairs: CH4 is tetrahedral (109.5°), NH3 trigonal pyramidal (~107°), H2O bent (~104.5°), CO2 linear (180°). Intermolecular forces, in increasing strength, are London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bonding (H bonded to N, O or F) explains water's high boiling point and holds DNA base pairs and protein secondary structures together.

topics.title: The Mole and Stoichiometry
topics.summary: Moles, molar mass, concentration, empirical formulae and balancing equations.

notes.b: One mole contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). Number of moles = mass ÷ molar mass. Molar mass is the relative formula mass in g/mol (e.g. NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol). At standard temperature and pressure, one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³. The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it (e.g. glucose C6H12O6 has empirical formula CH2O).

Molarity (mol/dm³) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in dm³. Dilution follows C1V1 = C2V2. Percentage w/v is grams per 100 mL: normal saline is 0.9% w/v NaCl (0.9 g in 100 mL, about 154 mmol/L). In balancing equations, the number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides; coefficients give mole ratios for calculations.

topics.title: Acids, Bases, pH and Buffers
topics.summary: Acid–base theories, pH calculations, neutralisation and buffer solutions in the body.

notes.b: Arrhenius acids release H+ in water; Brønsted–Lowry acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors; Lewis acids accept electron pairs. pH = −log10[H+]. At 25 °C neutral water has pH 7; acids have pH below 7 and bases above 7. A change of one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H+]. Strong acids (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3) ionise completely; weak acids (ethanoic acid, carbonic acid) only partially.

A buffer resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its salt). The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]). The bicarbonate buffer (H2CO3/HCO3−) is the main extracellular buffer keeping blood pH at 7.35–7.45; haemoglobin, phosphate and protein buffers also contribute.

topics.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
topics.summary: Hydrocarbons, functional groups, isomerism and IUPAC naming.

notes.b: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated with single bonds; alkenes (CnH2n) have a C=C double bond and undergo addition reactions (e.g. decolourising bromine water); alkynes (CnH2n−2) have a triple bond. IUPAC names use the longest carbon chain (meth-1, eth-2, prop-3, but-4, pent-5, hex-6 carbons) with suffixes for the functional group. Benzene (C6H6) is aromatic with delocalised π electrons and undergoes substitution rather than addition.
k: Alkanes CnH2n+2; alkenes CnH2n; alkynes CnH2n−2

notes.b: Important functional groups are alcohols (–OH, e.g. ethanol), aldehydes (–CHO), ketones (C=O within a chain, e.g. propanone/acetone), carboxylic acids (–COOH), esters (–COO–), amines (–NH2) and amides (–CONH2). Isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements: structural isomers differ in bonding sequence; stereoisomers include geometric (cis/trans) isomers and optical isomers (enantiomers), which arise from a chiral carbon bonded to four different groups. Drug enantiomers may differ in activity (e.g. thalidomide).
k: Enantiomers can have different drug effects
